source.title: Grokking as the Transition from Lazy to Rich Training Dynamics
source.authors: Tanishq Kumar; Blake Bordelon; Samuel J. Gershman; Cengiz Pehlevan

page_placements.theme: Data and capacity thresholds beyond training-time delay

record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization and its proposed lazy-to-rich mechanism, and presents results that challenge weight-norm/efficiency and optimizer-artifact explanations.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own grokking and feature-learning results. Results it attributes to cited papers are not recorded. Several plotted sweeps are described qualitatively; the paper does not report a systematic test of whether delay grows as the training set shrinks.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own grokking runs (modular-arithmetic MLP, polynomial regression, Gaussian eigenvector labels, MNIST, one-layer Transformer, student-teacher). It sweeps laziness (α, initial scale), weight decay and optimizer. It argues directly against weight-norm/efficiency (V5) and adaptive-optimizer (V7) accounts.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors argue grokking can arise from a transition from lazy (kernel) to rich (feature-learning) dynamics. It is controlled by output scale/laziness, initial NTK-task alignment, and a goldilocks dataset size. Weight decay and adaptive optimizers can amplify grokking but are neither necessary nor sufficient. They also state the lazy-to-rich transition is a sufficient, not necessary, mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and tests a lazy-to-rich feature-learning account rather than reproducing either original study's method; it uses polynomial regression as its main analyzable setting and additional modular-arithmetic, MNIST, Transformer, and student-teacher experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Output scale α, initial kernel-task alignment, dataset size, initialization scale, weight decay, task difficulty, and the threshold used to define regression accuracy change or qualify the reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Polynomial regression shows a goldilocks dataset size. P=50 fails to generalize, P=120 groks, P=500 train and test move together. In the eigenvector-label task, more data removes grokking for a fixed difficulty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delay occurs only in an intermediate dataset-size window; below it there is no generalization, above it train and test track.

record.problems: Many outcomes are presented as plots without numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not systematically measure delay versus shrinking training-set size. The student-teacher accuracy appearance depends on a threshold and is not accompanied by delayed generalization in loss. The authors state that adaptive-optimizer dynamics remain poorly understood.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the algorithmic training set shrinks. No training-fraction sweep on modular arithmetic.
No Fourier circuit identified for modular addition. No test of memorizing-component removal in the algorithmic task.
All of it: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Critical dataset size and ungrokking below it.
All of it: no comparison of algorithms across runs.
Softmax floating-point limits are not studied explicitly, only avoided via MSE. Adam-instability mechanisms are not characterized.

missing.what: Polynomial-regression α sweep: larger α lengthens the delay, small α removes grokking. Init-scale σ sweep has the same effect, with α~σ^-2 equivalence.
Initial NTK-task alignment ε controls the delay; low ε gives longer delay but lower final loss. The phase diagram gives time-to-grok over α and ε.
Grokking induced on Gaussian data by choosing NTK-eigenvector labels: j=1 generalizes immediately, j=70 groks, j=100 fails.
One-layer Transformer on modular addition (AdamW): α sweep makes grokking vanish at α=0.15 or become more drastic.
Modular-arithmetic MLP α sweep (vanilla GD) continuously controls grokking.
Adding a component of the solution to the initial weights removes grokking.
Transformer loss deviates from its linearization early despite grokking. Authors call lazy-to-rich sufficient but not necessary.
Grokking persists in polynomial regression with vanilla GD and MSE, in multi-index and Hermite variants; momentum keeps the same pattern.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Most outcomes are figure-only with no uncertainty. The modular-arithmetic delay in Fig 16 is short. The paper is internally inconsistent on student-teacher loss curves (Fig 13b vs Fig 18). Many V3-relevant results lack rows.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not establish that the delay grows as the training set shrinks. Its dataset-size sweep is on a polynomial regression task and reports loss, not modular-arithmetic test accuracy.
It measures feature alignment and loss components in its toy setting, but does not identify a Fourier algorithm for modular addition or test removal of memorizing components.
It reports MNIST and student-teacher results, but not text or molecule data. Its one-layer Transformer result uses modular arithmetic, not non-algorithmic data.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
It challenges the lower-norm efficiency account and varies weight decay, but does not establish a critical dataset size or test ungrokking below it.
It does not compare whether independently trained networks converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
Vanilla-GD grokking bears on whether adaptive-optimizer instability is necessary; adaptive-optimizer and softmax floating-point explanations are not fully controlled or ruled out.

rows.subject: two-layer network on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition and report train/test accuracy and loss for the same run.
rows.measure: Train and test classification accuracy; train and test MSE
rows.baseline: Test accuracy is flat early in training; chance level not stated.
rows.value: Train accuracy reaches perfect classification in 2k epochs; test accuracy stays flat early and generalizes around 3-4k epochs. The text says the network does perfectly in classification accuracy; train loss continues falling after train accuracy is perfect.
rows.note: The paper says the same run's test loss crosses the level associated with perfect classification around 3-4k epochs. Numerical accuracy values are not stated.
rows.check: State is fine, but the delay in this Fig 16 run is short: train accuracy is perfect at ~2k epochs and test generalizes at ~3-4k. The longer Fig 2 run (p=23, 50k epochs) is not recorded as its own V1 row.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-set size and report train/test MSE learning curves.
rows.value: The authors describe this as too little data and report failure to generalize.
rows.note: This is a regression loss result, not test accuracy; it does not determine the V1 accuracy claim.
rows.check: Polynomial regression is not an algorithmic dataset, so the row does not bear on V1. The dataset-size finding belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-set size and report train/test MSE learning curves.
rows.value: The authors describe this as the intermediate, grokking regime.
rows.note: The text identifies this as grokking, but the plotted measure is loss rather than test accuracy.
rows.check: Same as R2: non-algorithmic task, MSE only.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-set size and report train/test MSE learning curves.
rows.value: The authors describe this as full generalization, with learning curves moving together.
rows.note: This is not an accuracy result and does not show that delay grows monotonically as the training set shrinks.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Track the test-loss decomposition and feature alignment during grokking.
rows.measure: Test MSE components, including alignment error and linear-component error; feature alignment
rows.value: The paper reports an initial linear-component error followed by improved feature alignment; it says alignment begins around 1-2k epochs and the delayed test-loss fall follows.
rows.note: This supports gradual feature-learning progress in this toy setting, not the specific modular-addition circuit claim.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Compare nonlinear-network learning curves with lazy-network and initial-NTK regression curves.
rows.measure: Train/test loss and initial-NTK regression test loss
rows.value: The network initially tracks the linearized dynamics, then departs from them as features are learned and test loss improves late in training.
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence for a lazy-to-rich transition; it does not measure a memorizing circuit being removed.

rows.subject: MLP on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Vary output-scale parameter α to control grokking.
rows.baseline: Other α settings in the sweep; exact reference value not stated.
rows.value: The authors state that grokking vanishes at α = 0.0001.
rows.note: The numeric curve values are shown in the figure; the text explicitly reports disappearance at this α.

rows.subject: MLP on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Vary output-scale parameter α to control grokking.
rows.baseline: Other α settings in the sweep
rows.value: The authors describe grokking as continuously controlled by α; individual curve values are figure-only.
rows.note: The paper says the sweep changes grokking continuously; it does not give numerical outcomes for each plotted setting in the text.
rows.check: The authors say α continuously controls grokking on MNIST, which is the V3 effect in full. Partial is wrong.

rows.subject: student-teacher MLP
rows.stage_stated: student trained to match teacher outputs
rows.operation_detail: Vary output-scale parameter α and report threshold-defined accuracy.
rows.measure: Train/test accuracy, defined by being within 0.001 of the teacher label
rows.baseline: Other α settings; exact reference value not stated.
rows.value: The authors state that taking α small can make the apparent accuracy grokking vanish.
rows.note: The authors later explain that this regression-task accuracy measure can create an apparent grokking curve depending on threshold.
rows.check: Accuracy here is threshold-defined. The authors call the apparent grokking a threshold mirage (Figs 17-18), so the α effect on accuracy cannot show a real delay.

rows.subject: student-teacher MLP
rows.stage_stated: student trained to match teacher outputs
rows.operation_detail: Vary output-scale parameter α and report threshold-defined accuracy.
rows.measure: Train/test accuracy, defined by being within 0.001 of the teacher label
rows.baseline: Other α settings; exact reference value not stated.
rows.value: The authors say increasing α can make the apparent grokking more pronounced.
rows.note: The later loss analysis says this task's accuracy-based appearance is not accompanied by delayed generalization in loss.

rows.subject: student-teacher MLP
rows.stage_stated: student trained to match teacher outputs
rows.operation_detail: Compare train and test loss on the student-teacher task.
rows.baseline: Train loss compared with test loss
rows.value: The authors state that train loss tracks test loss throughout; they characterize the accuracy-based grokking appearance as a threshold artifact.
rows.note: This qualifies the student-teacher accuracy result: the paper reports no corresponding delayed generalization in loss.
rows.check: State fine. Note the paper is inconsistent: Fig 13(b)/Sec 14 describes student-teacher loss curves as showing delayed generalization, while Fig 18 says train loss tracks test loss throughout.

source_check.problem: Supported by Figure 18, although Section 14 describes student-teacher loss curves as delayed generalization.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Train without weight decay and track parameter weight norm.

conditions.value: addition modulo p; figure uses p = 23

rows.value: Parameter weight norm increases during training, including as the network generalizes.
rows.note: The authors present this as a counterexample to an account requiring a lower-norm generalizing solution.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5. Total parameter norm increases during grokking without weight decay; relative circuit efficiency at matched loss is not measured.
source_check.problem: Increasing total norm relative to initialization does not establish reversal of V5's relative low-norm circuit preference.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on polynomial regression
rows.operation_detail: Train with zero weight decay and track parameter weight norm.
rows.value: The authors state that parameter weight norm increases as the model groks.
rows.note: The paper says the final generalizing solution can have higher parameter norm than the initial solution.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5. Polynomial regression groks with increasing total norm and zero weight decay; relative circuit efficiency is not measured.
source_check.problem: A higher final norm than initialization does not show that the generalizing circuit is less efficient than a competing memorizing circuit.

rows.subject: one-layer Transformer on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Vary weight decay, then increase α while holding weight decay fixed.
rows.measure: Train/test cross-entropy loss and delay to generalization
rows.value: The authors describe a large grokking delay.
rows.note: This is a weight-decay effect on timing, not a test of the proposed efficient-circuit account.
rows.check: This is the reference condition (wd=1, α=0.5). Alone it shows grokking with weight decay but does not test V5's effect.

rows.subject: one-layer Transformer on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Increase weight decay while holding α fixed.
rows.measure: Train/test cross-entropy loss and delay to generalization
rows.value: The authors say grokking vanishes as increased weight decay encourages immediate NTK movement.
rows.note: The paper says increasing α to 1.4 with weight decay held at 5 recovers grokking.
rows.check: Higher weight decay removing the delay is consistent with weight decay pushing toward generalization. That is the V5 direction, not absence.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5. At alpha=0.5, increasing weight decay from 1 to 5 removes the delay; efficient-circuit selection is not measured.
source_check.problem: Faster generalization under stronger decay alone does not establish V5's circuit-efficiency mechanism.

rows.subject: one-layer Transformer on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Increase α while holding weight decay at 5.
rows.measure: Train/test cross-entropy loss and delay to generalization
rows.value: The authors say the increase in laziness recovers grokking.
rows.note: This shows that the timing changes with the combination of weight decay and output scale.
rows.check: This bears on V3: output scale (laziness) switches grokking back on at fixed weight decay. It is not a direct V5 test.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on modular arithmetic
rows.operation_detail: Train the modular-arithmetic model without an adaptive optimizer or weight decay.

conditions.value: addition modulo p; figure uses p = 23

rows.value: The authors report grokking with vanilla gradient descent and zero weight decay.
rows.note: This shows adaptive-optimizer instability is not necessary for grokking in the settings tested; it does not control every numerical explanation.
rows.check: V7's effect (the delay disappears once optimizer/numerics are controlled) does not occur. Grokking persists with vanilla GD, no weight decay, and MSE loss, so no softmax is involved.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: zero weight decay, vanilla GD, modular arithmetic MLP and polynomial regression
source_check.reason: R12–R13 refute necessary total-norm contraction and necessary explicit decay, but V5 permits other low-norm biases and concerns relative circuit efficiency. Increasing norm from initialization does not test that efficiency preference; the authors' broader interpretation exceeds these measurements.

relationships.condition: one-layer Transformer, AdamW, weight-decay × α sweep
relationships.reason: Higher weight decay removes the delay (R15), but raising laziness α restores it at fixed weight decay (R16). The authors read weight decay as acting via leaving the lazy regime (R14-R16).
relationships.display_finding: Higher weight decay removed the delay, but increasing laziness α restored it at fixed decay; the authors attributed decay's effect to leaving the lazy regime.

source_check.reason: Figure 12 measures timing under decay and output-scale interventions, without measuring relative circuit efficiency or showing failure of its predictions. Untested mechanism components cannot justify limits_scope; the scale-switch result supports V3.

relationships.reason: The delay persists without adaptive optimizers or softmax/cross-entropy, so these are not necessary for grokking here (R17).

relation.reason: Reports grokking trajectories, feature diagnostics, and controlled output-scale, alignment, data-size, and weight-decay interventions.

tranche.reason: Own experiments and explicit arguments contest necessary norm contraction and adaptive-optimizer explanations and qualify a universal lazy-to-rich account.

source_check.notes: Figure 6(a)'s caption gives alpha=0.0001, whereas its extracted legend lists 0.001. Section 14 and Figure 18 conflict on student-teacher loss delays; Section 14 also explicitly calls lazy-to-rich dynamics sufficient but unnecessary.

statements.problem: Accurately reports Figure 18; Section 14 contains a conflicting characterization of student-teacher loss dynamics.

statements.correction: Modular-addition and polynomial-regression MLPs grok under vanilla GD with zero weight decay; total norm increases; final norm exceeds initialization norm; relative circuit efficiencies are unmeasured.
statements.problem: The reported counterexamples challenge required total-norm contraction, but the V5 challenges label extends that result to relative circuit efficiency.

statements.correction: Figure 12: alpha=0.5, decay=1 gives a large delay; decay=5 removes it; alpha=1.4 restores it at decay=5. Circuit efficiency is unmeasured.
statements.problem: The Transformer timing result is correct, but output-scale compensation does not establish a limitation of V5's efficiency mechanism.
